html:
The Yudjá, or Juruna, are an Indigenous people of Brazil who once held the islands and banks of the Xingu River, a great southern tributary of the Amazon. They speak a language of the Tupian family.

They were canoe people: skilled boatmen who fished, hunted and grew manioc along the river. From the 1600s Portuguese missions, slavers and later the rubber boom pushed upriver, and epidemics and raids cut their numbers sharply.

Today they live in two groups. A northern group near Altamira, at the big bend of the Xingu, was hit hard by the Belo Monte dam, finished in the 2010s. A more traditional southern group lives in the Xingu Indigenous Park upriver. Their downstream neighbours included the Kuruaya and the Asurini of the Xingu.
